column2: Imagine four checkout lanes drawn on this board. Every incoming job carries two addresses picked independently from the four lanes. We can send the job to the first address, or peek at both and take the shorter line. The jobs and addresses are the same on both sides of the screen.

On the left, use the first letter of each pair. Three jobs land in A and one in B. On the right, choose the shorter of the two, using the first letter to break a tie. The first three land in A, C, and B. The last pair is A D. Where will that job go?

A already has a job. D is empty. The last job goes to D, so each lane ends up with one. Both sides saw the same four pairs. The difference is that the rule on the right could act on its second address.

That was one history. We need to know how often a rule helps, why it helps, and what happens if those little queue counters are out of date. To do that, keep the same pairs on both screens and let the math choose the next scene.

Suppose the current loads are two, one, zero, zero. Call a lane overloaded if it receives a third job. With just the first address we overload whenever A appears first. There are four such pairs out of sixteen equally likely ordered pairs.

With two addresses, any second lane besides A offers a way out. Both addresses have to say A. That leaves one pair out of sixteen. So this one state gives an exact change from one quarter to one sixteenth.

Here is the general version. Color the fraction f of lanes that are already too long. One uniform look fails with probability f. With two independent uniform looks, failure means landing in that colored set on both draws. The probability is f squared.

This calculation holds with replacement, which is why A A appears in the table. With sampling without replacement the second draw has different odds. The routing rule also changes the future loads, so the fraction f can diverge between the two screens.

To see a whole finite experiment, let each of four jobs carry one of the sixteen possible pairs. Call the ordered list of pairs a tape. There are sixty-five thousand five hundred and thirty-six equally likely tapes. Run both rules on each one and count how often the final maximum reaches three.

With one choice, that happens in thirteen thousand three hundred and twelve histories, about twenty point three one percent. With two choices, it happens in fourteen hundred and fifty-six, about two point two two percent. This test holds assignments in place for all four arrivals, with no service yet.
Can two choices ever lose on the exact same pairs? Try B B, B A, A A, A A. The first job goes to B on both boards. Where does the shorter-line rule send the second job, B A?

B has one job and A is empty, so the shorter-line rule sends job two to A. The last two jobs both say A A, and both must go to A. First-address routing ends with two in A and two in B. The shorter-line rule ends with three in A and one in B.

If the shorter-line rule breaks ties in favor of the first address, there are ninety-six reversals like this. Break ties in favor of the second address, and there are nine hundred and forty-eight. The distribution of the largest pile stays the same. Which exact histories lose can change, even when the overall odds do not.

Now let real queues drain as well as fill. Replace each checkout lane with a server that handles one job at a time. Watch one server receive three jobs at times zero, one, and four. Their service times are two, two, and one.

The first starts immediately and finishes at time two. The second arrives at time one and waits one unit, then finishes at time four. The third arrives as that service ends and waits zero. The average wait is one third of a unit.

For each arriving job we look at its chosen server's last scheduled finish time. If that is in the future, the difference is the waiting time. Its own service comes afterward. An idle server starts work immediately. That same calculation powers the larger simulation.

Now picture a very large cluster of identical servers. Jobs arrive as a Poisson process, with independent exponential service times of mean one. The mean arrival rate per server is lambda, below one. Write s sub k for the fraction of servers holding at least k jobs, including the one in service.

Count only jobs in position k or later in each queue. An arrival adds one to this count if it joins a queue that already has at least k minus one jobs. With d independent looks and the shortest choice, all d of the sampled queues must meet that threshold. In the large-system model this happens at rate lambda times s sub k minus one raised to d, per server.

A service completion removes one job from the count whenever that queue started with at least k jobs. In this example the long lane drops from four jobs to three, so one position at or above k disappears. The rate per server is s sub k. At equilibrium, the two rates balance.

Everyone has at least zero jobs, so s sub zero is one. For one look, every new level multiplies the previous level by lambda. For two looks, we square the previous level and then multiply by lambda. The exponents are one, three, seven, and fifteen. Each doubles and grows by one.

At a load of zero point eight five, the limiting fraction with at least three jobs is about sixty-one point four percent for one look and thirty-two point one percent for two. This is a statement about the stationary, large-cluster model. Four-job experiments and finite simulations have their own denominators.

Use a cluster of twenty-four servers now. Generate thirty thousand arrivals in each run at eighty-five percent nominal load. Let five thousand jobs warm the queues, then measure waiting times for the rest. Repeat on six separately seeded histories. Keep the arrivals, service times, and probe pairs fixed across policies within each history.

Compare the first address, the shorter of two, and the shortest of all twenty-four. The last rule keeps the first address if it ties for shortest. Otherwise it takes the lowest-numbered server among the shortest. For each run, find the wait that at least ninety-nine percent of measured jobs stay within. Then average those six percentiles.

The numbers are about thirty point two five, six point eight seven, and three point one zero mean service times. Looking everywhere wins this comparison with current information. The all-server policy is our strongest baseline here, and it makes the next result more interesting.

Imagine the scheduler publishes a bulletin board once per interval. Between updates, arrivals read the same queue lengths even when some of those queues have just accepted work. A short line on the board can attract a crowd while its actual line grows.

Refresh once every quarter of a mean service time. On average a little over five jobs arrive across the cluster in that interval. In the same six-history replay, the all-server waiting percentile grows to ten point one nine. Two choices comes in at seven point one seven.

At a refresh period of two mean service times, roughly forty-one arrivals see each bulletin. With our tie rule, the all-server mean percentile rises to forty-five point three, above the first-address baseline. Two choices has worsened as well, to eight point seven. Change only the all-server tie rule to a uniform draw among tied minima, and that percentile falls to twenty-six point zero two, below the first-address result of thirty point two five. A particular stale row is available only to arrivals whose probe pairs include it.

At thirty mean service times between updates, two choices gives twenty-seven point nine nine against thirty point two five for the first address, averaged over six runs. The shorter-of-two rule does better in four runs and worse in two. That is a close comparison in this replay. A different workload or update rule needs its own measurement.

Staleness affects the values we read. Correlation can affect where we look. Imagine the second address is forced to repeat the first with probability q. The rest of the time, it is an independent uniform draw. This is a model of two probes that sometimes share one source.

The failure probability now has two parts. With probability q, you get one effective look, with failure probability f. Otherwise you still get the f squared calculation. Add q times f to the quantity one minus q, multiplied by f squared.

If one quarter of queues are long and half the pairs are forced repeats, the bad event has probability five thirty-seconds, about fifteen point six percent. Independent pairs gave one sixteenth, or six point two five percent. Two addresses can contain much less than two independent looks.

There is another way to have a truthful but unhelpful counter. One server holds a long job with seven point seven five time units remaining. A second server holds two short jobs with a quarter unit left in each. The first line has fewer jobs. The second line has only half a time unit of work ahead of you.

A shortest-count rule sends the new arrival behind the one big job. A rule using known remaining service sends it behind the two short jobs. The wait in this worked state changes from seven point seven five to zero point five. Seen in the picture, the queue has both a head count and a length measured in time.

In practice we may have to estimate remaining work, and we may pay to get each estimate. Decide what a probe actually measures before treating it as a reliable vote. The simple count rule has a useful mathematical guarantee in the ideal model. Other observations call for their own model and their own checks.

Return to the two copies of the first four jobs. One extra independent look gives a job another way around a busy queue. The same calculation becomes a square in the large-cluster balance equation. That's why the far end of the queue distribution can shrink so sharply.

Return to the bulletin board. A scheduler that sees every row can still work from old counts. How old are the readings? What do they measure? How does the scheduler choose among tied rows? Those details can change the comparison even when the same jobs arrive.

If you want to test this on a system you run, replay the same arrivals and work sizes under three rules. Include one random address, two independent choices, and a strong baseline with the information you actually have. Measure the waiting distribution and the cost of the extra reads. The math tells us what to look for in that comparison.
